questions.qtext:
Consider a file system using $\textbf{single-level indexed allocation}$.
A file has $\textbf{100 blocks}$, and its index block is in memory.
To insert a block at position $50$, pointer shifting happens entirely in memory.

How many disk accesses are required?
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 0)
How the file update can be considered when the index block is not written back to disk

Block write - 1 disk access

Index File write back - 1 disk access

So there must be total of 2 disk access
Source solution 2 (score: 0)

It is a single level indexed allocation

To insert the block at position 50

we require 1 write to insert the block + all the pointers below it should be shifted which is 50 shifts
But Given that the shifting is entirely happens in the memory so no disk access.

So Answer is (A)

questions.qtext:
A file stored using $\textbf{linked allocation}$ has $\textbf{100 blocks}$.
We want to remove the $\textbf{50}^{\text{th}}$ block.
Only actual data block reads/writes count as disk accesses.

How many disk accesses are required?
questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 3)

To delete the 50th Block, linked allocation requires sequential traversal.
We must access the first 49 blocks to reach block \(49\).
Then we access block \(50\), and finally update the pointer of block \(49\).

Total disk accesses = \(49 + 1 + 1 = 51\).

Answer: B

Source solution 2 (score: 1)

To update the pointer of block 49, we need the address of block 51.

So to know where block 49 must point after removal, we must read block 50 to get the pointer to block 51.

  • Read blocks 1 → 50: You must follow the chain up to block 50. So total 50 reads.
  • Update block 49 pointer: You rewrite block 49 with pointer = address of block 51. So 1 write.
  • Mark block 50 as free: This updates the free-space structure on disk. So 1 more write.

( When block 50 is removed, the OS marks it as free in the free-list or bitmap. To do that, it updates the free-space structure on disk. Updating the free-space bitmap/freelist = 1 disk write. )

Source solution 3 (score: 0)

We begin by reading block 1 to find the address of block 2, and we repeat this sequential pointer traversal all the way until we reach and load the 50th block.

$$\text{Reads to find the target and its link} = \text{Blocks } [1, 2, 3, \dots, 50] \implies 50 \text{ reads}$$

Once the 50th block is loaded into RAM, we examine its pointer field to obtain the exact disk address of the 51st block.

At this stage, we have both the 49th block and the 50th block's internal link data available in memory.

In RAM, we update the next-pointer inside the 49th block to bypass block 50 and point straight to the 51st block's address.

We then write this modified 49th block back to its original sector on the disk to save the change:

$$\text{Total write accesses} = 1 \text{ (write back updated 49th block)}$$

Since the 50th block is being removed from the file chain, its physical data block does not need to be rewritten to the disk,

and any metadata freeing operations are handled in the file allocation table without counting as data block operations.

$$\text{Total accesses} = 50 \text{ reads} + 1 \text{ write} = 51$$

questions.qtext:
A file stored using linked allocation contains 100 blocks.
Block positions are numbered from 0 to 99, as is standard.

We want to remove the block at position 50.
Only the actual reads and writes of data blocks are counted as disk accesses.

How many disk accesses are required?
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 4)

We want to remove the block numbered 50 (i.e., the 51st block in the file).

In linked allocation, blocks are accessed one after another:

  • Read all earlier blocks — from the 1st block up to the 50th block → 50 reads
  • Then read the 51st block (the one being removed) to obtain the pointer to the next block → 1 read
  • Finally, update the pointer in the 50th block so it directly links to the block after the removed one → 1 write

Total disk accesses:
51 reads + 1 write = 52 accesses

Correct Answer: 52

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

In a standard singly linked list layout, a block only stores a pointer to its immediate successor.

This means block 49 only knows the address of block 50; it has no idea where block 51 is located on the disk.

To bypass block 50, the operating system must find out the disk address of block 51. The only way to discover this address is to physically read block 50 and look at its pointer field.

starting from the very first block at position 0:

$$\text{Blocks read: } \underbrace{0, 1, 2, \dots, 49}_{\text{Traversing to the target}} , \underbrace{50}_{\text{To get block 51's address}}$$

Counting the total number of blocks in the sequence from 0 to 50:

$$\text{Total reads} = 50 - 0 + 1 = 51 \text{ reads}$$

Once block 50 is read, block 51's address is known in RAM. The OS updates the pointer inside block 49 to point directly to block 51 and writes block 49 back to the disk, adding exactly 1 write operation.

$$\text{Total Accesses} = 51 \text{ reads} + 1 \text{ write} = 52$$
